sites.name: Site01 Connecting ridge (Barker 2021 RoI 4)
sites.subtitle: PGDA Site01 · Barker 2021 RoI 4

location.name: Site01 Connecting ridge (Barker 2021 RoI 4)

sites.description: A ridge at the Moon's south pole, about 17 km from the pole, connecting the rims of Shackleton crater and de Gerlache crater (Barker et al. 2021). Because it is high and close to the pole, where the Sun always stays near the horizon, parts of it see the Sun most of the time: Mazarico et al. (2011) ranked it first of the south polar sites for average illumination (their site 1), and Barker et al. (2021) studied it as a potential landing site. They found seven regions on it where, at 1 m above the ground in 2024-2025, more than 70% of the Sun's disc is in view on average. The point used here is the centre of the largest, region 4.
sites.source: Barker, M. K., et al. (2021), Planet. Space Sci. 203, 105119, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119, Table 2: centroid of Site01 region of interest 4, polar stereographic x = -11.2875 km, y = -12.1675 km (89.452675 S, 222.851347 E), in the PGDA product 78 Site01 DEM tile. Site01 (Connecting ridge) is site 1 of Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Icarus 211, 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030.

sites.name: Site06 Nobile rim 1 (Mazarico 2011 site 6)
sites.subtitle: PGDA Site06 · Mazarico 2011 rank 6

location.name: Site06 Nobile rim 1 (Mazarico 2011 site 6)

sites.description: A point on the rim of Nobile crater, about 143 km from the Moon's south pole. Mazarico et al. (2011) listed the 50 most illuminated spots near the south pole on a 240 m map; this one ranks 6th, with 86% of the Sun's disc in view on average at surface level over 1970-2044. Barker et al. (2021) made the 5 m map of the site (PGDA product 78) that is used here. The point is Mazarico's published coordinate, given to 0.01 degrees (about 300 m in latitude). On the 5 m map used here, the point is on an 8° slope. The Sun never rises more than about 6° above the horizon here, and close to the ground the slope beside the point hides it: in 2028, at 1 m above the ground, 41% of the Sun's disc is in view on average (some of the Sun is in view 47% of the time), rising to 83% at 5 m and 87% at 10 m. Mazarico's 240 m map is too coarse to show this slope; repeating their method on a 240 m map gives 87% at 10 m, close to their 87%.
sites.source: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Icarus 211, 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030, Table 3 (south pole, rank 6): 37.07 E, 85.30 S (polar stereographic x = 85.958 km, y = 113.780 km on the 1737.4 km sphere). Site name and 5 m map: PGDA product 78 (Barker, M. K., et al. (2021), Planet. Space Sci. 203, 105119, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119).

sites.name: Site20 Leibnitz beta plateau (Mazarico 2011 site 20)
sites.subtitle: PGDA Site20 · Mazarico 2011 rank 20

location.name: Site20 Leibnitz beta plateau (Mazarico 2011 site 20)

sites.description: A point on the Leibnitz beta plateau, about 139 km from the Moon's south pole. Mazarico et al. (2011) listed the 50 most illuminated spots near the south pole on a 240 m map; this one ranks 20th, with 82% of the Sun's disc in view on average at surface level over 1970-2044. Barker et al. (2021) made the 5 m map of the site (PGDA product 78) that is used here. The point is Mazarico's published coordinate, given to 0.01 degrees (about 300 m in latitude). On the maps used here, this coordinate lies on the side of the plateau rather than its best-lit ground. Repeating Mazarico's method there gives about 25% of the Sun's disc in view at surface level (46% at 10 m), against their 82% (83%). The two nearest points of a 240 m grid, 85 and 158 m away, do no better than 58% at 10 m, so the published coordinate is kept. On the 5 m map in 2028, 14% of the Sun's disc is in view on average at 1 m above the ground (some of the Sun is in view 17% of the time) and 30% at 10 m. Results for this site describe that point.
sites.source: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Icarus 211, 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030, Table 3 (south pole, rank 20): 31.73 E, 85.43 S (polar stereographic x = 72.919 km, y = 117.928 km on the 1737.4 km sphere). Site name and 5 m map: PGDA product 78 (Barker, M. K., et al. (2021), Planet. Space Sci. 203, 105119, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119).

sites.name: Site23 Malapert massif (Mazarico 2011 site 23)
sites.subtitle: PGDA Site23 · Mazarico 2011 rank 23

location.name: Site23 Malapert massif (Mazarico 2011 site 23)

sites.description: A point on the Malapert massif, about 122 km from the Moon's south pole. Mazarico et al. (2011) listed the 50 most illuminated spots near the south pole on a 240 m map; this one ranks 23rd, with 82% of the Sun's disc in view on average at surface level over 1970-2044. Mazarico et al. (2011) also note that high ground such as Mons Malapert has good visibility of the Earth. Barker et al. (2021) made the 5 m map of the site (PGDA product 78) that is used here. The point is Mazarico's published coordinate, given to 0.01 degrees (about 300 m in latitude). On the 5 m map used here, the point is on a 7° slope. The Sun never rises more than about 6° above the horizon here, and close to the ground the slope beside the point hides it: in 2028, at 1 m above the ground, 45% of the Sun's disc is in view on average (some of the Sun is in view 52% of the time), rising to 67% at 2 m and 82% at 5 m and 10 m. Mazarico's 240 m map is too coarse to show this slope; repeating their method on a 240 m map gives 82% at 10 m, close to their 83%. The Earth is in view 51% of 2028 at 1 m and 82% at 10 m, the most of the eight PGDA sites at that height.
sites.source: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Icarus 211, 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030, Table 3 (south pole, rank 23): 357.70 E, 85.97 S (polar stereographic x = -4.906 km, y = 122.155 km on the 1737.4 km sphere). sites.name: Peak near Cabeus B (Artemis III candidate region, NASA 2024)
sites.subtitle: Artemis III candidate region · NASA, Oct 2024

location.name: Peak near Cabeus B (Artemis III candidate region, NASA 2024)

sites.description: One of nine regions near the Moon's south pole that NASA named on 28 October 2024 as candidate landing regions for Artemis III, each containing several potential landing sites. In February 2026 NASA made Artemis III a crewed test flight in Earth orbit in 2027, with the first landing planned for Artemis IV in 2028; NASA's Artemis IV page (updated March 2026) still shows these nine regions. NASA does not give a centre for each region. The point used here is the centre of the 1 km navigation grid the U.S. Geological Survey made for the region (McClernan 2024), about 21 by 21 km; the centre is this project's calculation from the USGS grid and is about 193 km from the pole. It is a geometric centre, not a landing site.
sites.source: Region: NASA (2024), NASA Provides Update on Artemis III Moon Landing Regions, release 24-136, 28 October 2024, https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-provides-update-on-artemis-iii-moon-landing-regions/. Point: centre of the region's 1 km grid in McClernan, M. T. (2024), Down Selected Artemis III Candidate Landing Site Navigational Grids, U.S. Geological Survey data release, doi:10.5066/P1MEQ6UK (Peak_Near_Cabeus_B.zip, Peak_Near_Cabeus_B_PolarLGRS_ACC_1km_S_Grid: lunar polar stereographic easting 311-332 km, northing 559-580 km; false easting and northing 500 km, scale factor 0.994, 1737.4 km sphere). The centre, 83.651364 S, 68.726263 W, is this project's calculation (the release does not state the frame; mean Earth assumed, not yet checked). Mission change: NASA release 26-022, 27 February 2026, https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-adds-mission-to-artemis-lunar-program-updates-architecture/; NASA Artemis IV page, https://www.nasa.gov/mission/artemis-iv/ (updated 16 March 2026).
